newsitem.title: UK: Building stocks still have upside as housing surges.
newsitem.headline: Building stocks still have upside as housing surges.

text.p: Britain's housing market is back with a vengeance as prices rise at the fastest rate since 1988 and some analysts say there's still time for stock investors to cash in on the sector despite election uncertainty and a possible interest rate hike.

Last week the Royal Institute of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) said house prices had shot up by more than five percent in the three months to March -- the first time this has happened in 20 years apart from 1988 when the market boomed and then busted soon after.

"The housing market seems immune to decline," RICS spokesman Ian Perry said. "Even the widely-predicted interest rate rise in early May and possible phasing out of MIRAS (mortgage interest tax relief) is unlikely to have any appreciable effect."
Political uncertainty is another factor which has failed to dent the market's confidence in the run-up to the May 1 election which the opposition Labour Party is widely tipped to win.

Building companies linked to the domestic housing market have performed better than some other construction and building material firms with exposure to tougher markets overseas -- notably in Germany and France.
Stock analysts say there is still scope for gains with companies in British housebuilding and with high exposure to the domestic building materials sectors.
"I think there's still real value to be had with the housebuilders," said one industry analyst.
"The shares have come back an awful long way. But there was a wobble recently as some people locked in profits, looking ahead to the election and a possible rate rise afterwards."
But the building analyst said the sector would remain in vogue even if the market faced a possible rate rise of between a half and one percent on base rates.
The key issue when choosing housebuilders, he said, was the quality of their land bank. Land prices are experiencing double digit inflation, outpacing even house price inflation.
"Those housebuilders with poor land banks will not be able to pass the full scale of land inflation on but may take a hit on their margins instead," he said.

SocGen's Howard Proctor believes the housebuilding sector is tougher hunting ground for investors on the lookout for bargains, making material firms more attractive. Even so, the market backdrop looked good, he said.

"With both housing transactions and prices running over seven percent ahead of last year, purchaser confidence still strong ahead of an election and relatively low cost inflation, the sector can look forward to some very bullish statements and numerous profit upgrades," said Proctor.
"Yet it is becoming increasingly hard to find value in a sector where virtually all the quality stocks have outperformed strongly over the last year," he said.

For that reason Proctor is laying his bets on "the biggest long-term beneficiaries of housing starts -- the second line material stocks". He favours companies like Caradon Plc, Hepworth Plc and Rugby Group Plc.

Mike Betts, at Goldman Sachs, said: "There probably is quite a lot more to come. I would look at the building material companies with high U.K. exposures -- Caradon and Tarmac (Plc) will definitely be major beneficiaries, although influenced by other geographical markets."
Another possible boost could be the estimated 20 billion pounds ($33 billion) in windfalls for shareholders in the several building societies converting into banks this year.
Betts said this should partly feed through to household repair and maintenance as well as encouraging people to move or buy a house.
He added that the overall house price rises to date were due to lack of supply, adding that once more homes came on to the market the key indicator of sales volumes should then start picking up.
Latest RICS figures showed housing market transactions at a low 1.3 million per year compared with the 2.2 million per year rate seen in 1988.
($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
